title: Permutations
directAnswer: Return every ordering of the array. Unlike subsets/combinations, ORDER matters and every element is used exactly once — so there is NO start index. Instead track which elements are already in the path with a `used[]` boolean array (or a set), loop `i` from 0 every level, skip used elements, choose → recurse → un-choose. There are n! permutations, so the answer is O(n · n!).

remember.pattern: Backtracking with a used[] set, no start index (choose → explore → un-choose)
remember.formula:
def backtrack(path):
    if len(path) == len(nums): results.append(path[:]); return
    for i in range(len(nums)):          # always from 0 — order matters
        if used[i]: continue            # skip elements already in the path
        used[i] = True; path.append(nums[i])   # choose
        backtrack(path)                         # explore
        path.pop(); used[i] = False             # un-choose (restore BOTH)
rules: **No start index** — permutations care about order, so loop `i` from 0 at every level (the opposite of subsets/combinations).
Track membership with `used[]` (or a set) and `continue` on used elements — that's what stops an element appearing twice in one permutation.
Record only at a **complete leaf** (`len(path) == n`) — every permutation uses all n elements, so partial paths aren't answers.
On un-choose you must restore **both** `path.pop()` **and** `used[i] = false` — forgetting the second leaves the element permanently marked.
Append a **copy** `path[:]` — the shared path keeps mutating as you backtrack and would corrupt stored permutations.
There are exactly **n!** permutations — `O(n · n!)` is optimal; you cannot beat the output size.
whenToUse: Asked for **all orderings / arrangements** where sequence matters
Every element must be used exactly once (full-length results only)
Anagrams, seating arrangements, ordering tasks under no extra constraint
antiSignals: Order does **not** matter → that's Subsets/Combinations (use a start index instead of used[])
Only the **count** of orderings is needed → it's just n!, no enumeration
Input has duplicates and you must dedup → Permutations II (sort + skip same-level repeats)
n is large (> ~10–12) → n! explodes; the problem can't want full enumeration
remember.takeaway: Permutations is the 'order matters' member of the backtracking family. The defining edit vs Subsets is dropping the start index and adding a used[] set so every position can draw from any unused element. Master the choose/explore/un-choose with used-restoration here and Permutations II, N-Queens, and Combinations all reuse the same muscle.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know that order-matters problems drop the start index in favour of a used[] set, and whether you correctly restore BOTH the path and the used flag on backtrack. Bonus: recognising n! as the lower bound so O(n · n!) is optimal.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Keeping a start index (which produces combinations, not permutations), forgetting to reset `used[i] = false` after recursion (so later branches think the element is taken), or recording partial paths instead of only full-length ones.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Contrast permutations vs subsets explicitly — 'order matters, so no start index; I track used elements instead'. State n! as the lower bound, write clean choose/explore/un-choose, and mention the in-place swap variant that avoids the used[] array.

problemStatement: Given an array `nums` of **distinct** integers, return **all the possible permutations**. You can return the answer in **any order**.
constraints: All the integers of nums are unique
understanding: Produce every ordering of the array — all n! arrangements that use each element exactly once. Because the elements are distinct, the only source of duplicates would be revisiting an element, which the used[] check prevents. [1,2,3] and [2,1,3] are distinct answers because order is part of the identity of a permutation.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the integers distinct, or can there be duplicates?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Distinct. With duplicates we'd need an extra dedup step (sort + skip equal siblings) — that's Permutations II (LC 47).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does every permutation use all n elements?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — a permutation is a full reordering, so each result has length n. We only record when the path reaches length n.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the order of the output list matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, any order of the permutations is accepted. But within each permutation, order is the whole point — [1,2,3] ≠ [3,2,1].

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can n get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: At most 6, so 6! = 720 permutations — tiny. The small bound signals that exponential/factorial enumeration is the intended solution.

examples.explanation: All 3! = 6 orderings. Note both [1,2,3] and [3,2,1] appear — order distinguishes them.
Two permutations. 0 is a valid element; we test the used flag, not the value, so 0 causes no issue.
A single element has exactly one permutation — itself.

approaches.name: Backtracking with a used[] Set (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The canonical answer. Phrase it as 'order matters so no start index — I draw any unused element at each position, tracked with a used[] array'.
hints: There are n! permutations. Think of filling positions left to right: position 0 can be any element, position 1 any of the remaining, and so on. What do you need to remember to know which elements remain?
Unlike subsets, order matters, so don't use a start index — at every level loop `i` from 0 and skip elements already placed. A boolean `used[]` (or a set) tracks what's in the current path.
Choose: mark `used[i] = true` and append nums[i]. Explore: recurse. Un-choose: pop AND set `used[i] = false`. Record a copy only when the path length equals n.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are n! leaves (complete permutations) and the tree has fewer than n·n! internal nodes total. At each of the n! leaves we copy a length-n path, costing O(n). So total time is O(n · n!). Extra space beyond the output is the recursion depth (n), the path (n), and used[] (n) — all O(n).
approaches.explanation:
Fill the permutation position by position. At each call, loop `i` over **all** indices from 0; if `nums[i]` is already in the path (`used[i]` is true) skip it, otherwise **choose** it (mark used, append), **explore** by recursing, then **un-choose** (pop and unmark). When the path reaches length n we've placed every element, so we record a copy and return.

**Why there is no start index — the key contrast with Subsets.** In subsets/combinations the start index enforces non-decreasing order so {1,2} and {2,1} aren't both emitted. But for permutations [1,2] and [2,1] are *different valid answers* — we *want* both. So we must allow each position to draw from any element, which means looping from 0 every level. The price of dropping the start index is that we can no longer use position to know what's been used; we need explicit bookkeeping, which is exactly what `used[]` provides.

**Why `used[]` is the right bookkeeping.** Each element must appear exactly once per permutation. `used[i]` answers 'is nums[i] already in the current path?' in O(1). When it's true we `continue`, guaranteeing no element is placed twice. A `set` of values works too when elements are distinct, but a boolean array indexed by position is cleaner and also handles the duplicate-value case the moment you graduate to Permutations II.

**Why you must restore BOTH on un-choose.** The single most common bug here is asymmetric backtracking. Choosing does two things — `used[i] = true` and `path.append` — so un-choosing must undo *both*: `path.pop()` and `used[i] = false`. Restore only the path and the element stays marked 'used' forever, so every later branch wrongly believes it's unavailable and you lose whole swaths of permutations. The choose and un-choose steps must be mirror images.

**Why we record only at a full-length leaf.** A permutation, by definition, is a complete arrangement of all n elements. Partial paths like [1,2] (when n = 3) are not answers — they're just internal nodes on the way to [1,2,3] and [1,3,... wait, that branch]. So the base case is `len(path) == n`, and we snapshot `path[:]` there. Appending the live `path` instead would store a reference that the subsequent pops mutate, corrupting every saved permutation.
approaches.insight: Permutations vs Subsets is the cleanest illustration of the two backtracking 'modes': when order is irrelevant, a start index moves forward only and needs no membership tracking; when order matters, you drop the start index and pay for a used[] set. Knowing which mode a problem is in — by asking 'is [1,2] the same as [2,1] here?' — tells you instantly which skeleton to write.

dryRun.intro: No start index — every level loops i from 0 and skips used elements. Record only when path length == 3. Watch how un-choose restores BOTH the path and the used flag.

code.python:
def permute(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    results: list[list[int]] = []
    used = [False] * len(nums)

    def backtrack(path: list[int]) -> None:
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            results.append(path[:])      # full-length leaf → record a COPY
            return
        for i in range(len(nums)):       # always from 0 — order matters
            if used[i]:
                continue                 # skip elements already in the path
            used[i] = True               # choose
            path.append(nums[i])
            backtrack(path)              # explore
            path.pop()                   # un-choose: restore BOTH
            used[i] = False

    backtrack([])
    return results

edgeCases.behavior: Root chooses 1 → path length 1 == n → record [1]. Returns [[1]]. The single-element base case.
Produces [0,1] and [1,0]. The used[] check (not a truthiness test) means element 0 is handled correctly.

pitfalls: Keeping a start index — turns the output into combinations (only [1,2], never [2,1]).
Forgetting `used[i] = false` on backtrack — the element stays marked and later branches lose permutations.
Recording partial paths instead of only length-n leaves — emits incomplete arrangements.
Appending `path` instead of `path[:]` — all stored permutations mutate to the same list.

commonMistakes: Using a start index (as in subsets), which yields combinations instead of permutations.
Forgetting to reset `used[i] = false` after the recursive call, so the element stays marked as used.
Storing the live `path` reference instead of a copy, so every permutation collapses to the same list.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Keeping a start index (gives combinations)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A start index forces forward-only picks, so you'd produce [1,2] but never [2,1]. Permutations need every ordering, so loop from 0 and track used elements instead.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
def backtrack(start, path):
    if len(path) == len(nums):
        results.append(path[:]); return
    for i in range(start, len(nums)):   # start index → combinations!
        path.append(nums[i])
        backtrack(i + 1, path)
        path.pop()

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting to reset used[i]
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Choosing sets `used[i] = True`. If un-choose pops the path but doesn't reset the flag, the element stays 'taken' for every sibling and ancestor branch, silently dropping most permutations.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
used[i] = True; path.append(nums[i])
backtrack(path)
path.pop()                # used[i] never reset!
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
used[i] = True; path.append(nums[i])
backtrack(path)
path.pop(); used[i] = False   # restore BOTH

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Storing the live path reference
commonMistakesDetailed.why: `results.append(path)` stores the same list; later pops mutate it, so every permutation ends up identical. Snapshot with `path[:]`.

followupVariations.title: Permutations II
followupVariations.hint: Input has duplicates → sort first, then skip `nums[i] == nums[i-1] && !used[i-1]` to avoid duplicate permutations at the same level.

followupVariations.title: Next Permutation
followupVariations.hint: Only the single next ordering in lexicographic sequence → O(n) in-place: find the pivot, swap with the next-larger suffix element, reverse the suffix. No backtracking.

followupVariations.title: Subsets
followupVariations.hint: Order does NOT matter → use a start index instead of used[], and record at every node rather than only full-length leaves.

followupVariations.title: Combinations
followupVariations.hint: Choose k of n where order doesn't matter → start-index template, record when path length == k.

patternNote: Canonical Backtracking for order-matters enumeration (choose → explore → un-choose) with a used[] set and NO start index. Recognise it whenever every arrangement is a distinct answer. The defining contrast with Subsets/Combinations — drop the start index, add used[] — also drives Permutations II and underlies the placement logic in N-Queens.
